title: Introduction to Pharmacology — Session 1

summary.text: Pharmacology studies how drugs interact with living systems: **pharmacokinetics** is what the body does to the drug (ADME), and **pharmacodynamics** is what the drug does to the body.
Learn and prescribe by **generic name** — brand names can hide a shared ingredient and cause unintentional double-dosing.
Drugs move from discovery through preclinical testing, **Phase I–III** trials, FDA review, and **Phase IV** postmarketing surveillance — where rare adverse effects are often first found.
Drugs act on five target classes; a **competitive antagonist** shifts the dose-response curve right (same Emax), while a **noncompetitive/irreversible** antagonist lowers Emax.

**Potency** (EC₅₀) is the dose needed and **efficacy** (Emax) is the ceiling — efficacy matters more — and narrow-TI drugs (**warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin**) need careful dosing and blood levels.
Oral drugs face **first-pass** hepatic metabolism that lowers bioavailability (IV = 100%), and distribution depends on protein binding, lipid solubility, perfusion, and barriers like the BBB.

chunks.text: **Pharmacology:** the scientific study of how drugs interact with living systems — from the molecular level to the whole patient.
**Drug (medication):** any chemical substance used to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent disease, or to alter a physiologic process.
**Pharmacologic effect:** a measurable biological change a drug produces (e.g., lower blood pressure).
**Therapeutic effect:** the intended, beneficial pharmacologic effect for a given condition.
**Adverse drug reaction (ADR):** an unintended and harmful response occurring at normal therapeutic doses.
**Toxicity:** harmful effects that occur as the dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.
**Chemical name:** describes the exact molecular structure (rarely used in clinical practice).
**Generic name:** the official, non-proprietary name assigned to the active drug — one generic name per drug, regardless of manufacturer.
**Brand (trade) name:** the manufacturer's marketed name; the same generic drug may have several brand names, and brand names change between countries.
**Prodrug:** an inactive precursor converted to the active drug in the body (usually by metabolism).
**Poisons** are drugs with almost exclusively harmful effects — but "the dose makes the poison" (Paracelsus): any substance can harm at the wrong dose.
Pharmacokinetics = what the body does to the drug — ADME.
Pharmacodynamics = what the drug does to the body — receptors & effect.
Pharmacogenomics = how genetic variation shapes individual drug response.
Clinical Pharmacology / Toxicology = applying PK/PD to real patients, and the study of poisoning.
This map covers the whole lecture: PK and PD are the two biggest buckets, and nearly everything else (toxicology, pharmacogenomics, therapeutics) sits on top of them.
**PA students should learn and prescribe by generic name — it is unambiguous, international, and avoids confusing a patient's multiple brand-name products for different drugs.**
Different brand-name products (Tylenol, many combination cold/flu products) can share the same active generic ingredient.
Prescribing and counseling by generic name avoids hiding duplicate therapy — the reason PAs default to generic names.
If a patient says they take "Tylenol" and separately "acetaminophen," check for accidental double-dosing — this previews the acetaminophen toxicity discussion.
Precise vocabulary (generic names, therapeutic vs. adverse effects) protects patients.
More than half of prescriptions in the USA are for generic drugs.
Acetaminophen (generic) is sold as Tylenol and under many store brands.
"Therapeutic effect" and "pharmacologic effect" are not synonyms — a drug can have pharmacologic effects that are not therapeutic (that is often exactly what an adverse effect is).
ADR vs. toxicity: an ADR happens at normal therapeutic doses; toxicity happens when dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.
Generic names do NOT vary by manufacturer (one per drug); brand names DO vary — and change between countries.

chunks.text: Why prescribe by generic name? One drug has ONE generic name but can hide under SEVERAL brand names — so brand-name products can conceal duplicate therapy and cause double-dosing.
Pharmaco**K**inetics = the body **K**eeps the drug moving (ADME). Pharmaco**D**ynamics = what the **D**rug **D**oes to the body.
ADR = **A**t normal **D**oses, **R**eaction is harmful. Toxicity = **T**oo much (exceeds the therapeutic range).
**Efficacy:** how well a drug works under ideal, controlled trial conditions.
**Effectiveness:** how well a drug works in everyday clinical practice, with real-world adherence and comorbidities.
Drug interactions can also reduce real-world effectiveness below trial efficacy.
**Benefit vs. risk:** the central question regulators and prescribers must weigh for every approval and every prescription.
**Adverse-event reporting:** ongoing, voluntary and mandatory reporting systems (e.g., FDA MedWatch) that catch safety signals after approval.
Where new drugs come from — Natural products: plants, fungi, microbes, marine organisms.
Synthetic & biotech: designed small molecules; recombinant proteins.
Biologics: monoclonal antibodies, gene- and cell-based therapies.
Drug repurposing: an existing approved drug found to treat a new condition.
From discovery to patient: Discovery → Preclinical testing → Clinical trials → FDA review → Approval → Postmarket surveillance.
Most candidate drugs fail somewhere along this pipeline — approval is the exception, not the rule.
Phase I: safety, tolerability, dose-finding — a small group of healthy volunteers.
Phase II: preliminary efficacy and side-effect profile — a few hundred patients with the target condition.
Phase III: confirm efficacy and monitor adverse effects at scale — hundreds to thousands of patients, often multi-site.
Phase IV: postmarketing surveillance after approval — the general prescribed population.
Every approved drug has passed through a structured development and regulatory pipeline (Phases I–IV).
Phase II has the **highest failure rate** — only about 25% of new drugs move on to Phase III.
Phase III usually enrolls **thousands** of patients (Figure 1–6: 1000–6000), often double-blind and crossover, in settings like the drug's eventual use.
Less than one-third of drugs studied in humans survive clinical trials and reach the market.
To see one case of a toxicity occurring 1 in 10,000, several hundred thousand patients may need exposure — so rare effects usually surface only in Phase IV, which has **no fixed duration**.
Marketing requires a **New Drug Application (NDA)** after Phase III; human testing starts only after an **IND** (Investigational New Drug) application.
Postmarketing surveillance (Phase IV) is where rare adverse effects are often first detected — trial populations are too small and too short in duration to catch 1-in-10,000 events.

Case: a new medication improves symptoms in 70% of patients with a chronic, non-life-threatening condition, but postmarketing data show serious hepatotoxicity in about 1%. **Would you prescribe it — and does your answer depend on what else is available?**

**Clinical pearl:** risk-benefit analysis is always comparative — a 1% serious-toxicity rate reads very differently if it is the only effective option versus if three safer alternatives already exist.
Ask "compared to what?" rather than judging the number in isolation.
A patent lasts 20 years; after it expires, generics are approved through an **abbreviated new drug application (ANDA)** that requires bioequivalence data.
Placebo responses can occur in as many as 30–40% of subjects — the reason controlled, blinded trials are needed.
Adverse events that are both **serious and unexpected** must be reported to the FDA within 15 days; clinicians can report through MedWatch.
FDA MedWatch — an adverse-event reporting system.
Biologic DMARDs (MSK unit, later) are a direct example of the "biotechnology" drug source.
**Thalidomide** (sold in Europe as a "nontoxic" hypnotic) caused about 10,000 birth defects and led to the **Kefauver-Harris Amendments (1962)**, which required proof of efficacy as well as safety.
The **Orphan Drug Amendment (1983)** gives incentives for drugs treating diseases with fewer than 200,000 US patients.
Efficacy vs. effectiveness is a favorite exam distinction: efficacy is the trial result; effectiveness is what happens once real patients with real adherence patterns use the drug.
Phase III — not Phase I, II, or IV — is the large pre-approval trial that confirms efficacy and monitors safety at scale.
Phase III is what most people picture as "the" clinical trial, but regulatory decisions already begin shaping the drug long before that.

Phase: Phase II · Primary purpose: Preliminary efficacy and side-effect profile · Typical population: A few hundred patients with the target condition · How to tell apart: First look at whether it works

What changes it · Efficacy: Not covered in materials · Effectiveness: Real-world adherence, comorbidities (and drug interactions — SG)
Shorthand · Efficacy: The trial result · Effectiveness: What happens with real patients

Phase I population: slides say Phase I: a small group of healthy volunteers. Textbook says Phase I: 20–100 healthy volunteers — but if significant toxicity is expected (cancer, AIDS therapy), volunteer **patients with the disease** are used instead.
Phase II size: slides say Phase II: a few hundred patients with the target condition. Textbook says Phase II: a modest number of patients (100–200) with the target disease.
Why are rare adverse effects found after approval? Trials are too small and too short to catch 1-in-10,000 events — so they show up in Phase IV, in the general prescribed population.
Phases by question: **I** = Is it safe (healthy volunteers)? **II** = Is there an effect? **III** = Is it confirmed at scale? **IV** = Is it still safe in everyone?
Effica**C**y = **C**ontrolled conditions. Effecti**V**eness = real-world **V**ariables (adherence, comorbidities).
**Drug target:** the specific molecule a drug binds to produce its effect.
**Receptor:** a protein target whose activation (or blockade) triggers a cellular response.
**Signal transduction:** the chain of molecular events that converts receptor binding into a cellular effect.
**Pharmacologic response:** the measurable downstream result — contraction, secretion, gene transcription, and so on.
Full agonist — maximal receptor activation.
Partial agonist — submaximal activation, even at full receptor occupancy.
Inverse agonist — reduces baseline (constitutive) receptor activity.
Competitive antagonist — reversibly competes with agonist at the same site; overcome by more agonist.
Noncompetitive antagonist — binds elsewhere or irreversibly reduces the maximal effect.
Irreversible antagonist — permanently inactivates the receptor until new receptor is synthesized.
The pathway: drug → target → signal transduction → response. Every pharmacodynamics topic for the rest of the course maps onto this chain.
Receptor concept: Drug + Receptor → Drug-Receptor Complex → Cellular Response.
This single chain underlies agonism, antagonism, potency, and efficacy — all describe different features of this interaction.
Five major drug target classes: receptors, ion channels, enzymes, transporters, nucleic acids.
Receptors: G-protein-coupled, ligand-gated ion channel, enzyme-linked, nuclear.
Ion channels: directly gate the flow of ions across a membrane.
Enzymes: drugs can inhibit or, less commonly, activate an enzyme's activity.
Transporters & nucleic acids: carrier proteins; or DNA/RNA for some antimicrobials & gene therapies.
Most drugs target receptors or enzymes — ion channels and transporters matter especially for cardiac and CNS drugs.
An inverse agonist actively reduces constitutive (baseline) receptor activity below normal; a true antagonist merely blocks the agonist without lowering baseline activity itself.
**Spare receptors:** a maximal response can occur without occupying every receptor (e.g., about 90% of cardiac β receptors can be blocked and maximal inotropic response still preserved).
**Irreversible antagonist** effects last until new receptors are made — duration depends on receptor turnover, not drug elimination (phenoxybenzamine for pheochromocytoma).
A partial agonist's lower maximal effect is **not** due to lower affinity — it can occupy all receptors and still produce less response.
**Allosteric modulators** bind a different site from the agonist (e.g., benzodiazepines enhance GABA's effect).
Agonist-induced **desensitization** (tachyphylaxis) and downregulation reduce response with continued exposure.
Albuterol is a selective β2-adrenergic receptor agonist.
Binding activates the β2 receptor → increases intracellular cAMP.
Rising cAMP relaxes bronchial smooth muscle → bronchodilation.
**This is the same receptor-to-response logic you will reuse for every agonist drug this term.**
Albuterol bridges introductory pharmacodynamics into the pulmonary pharmacology seen later in the curriculum.
Competitive antagonism is surmountable in real life: exercise or stress raises catecholamines enough to overcome a fixed propranolol dose.
Propranolol markedly slows the heart rate in pheochromocytoma (high catecholamines) but not the resting rate of a trained marathon runner.
Albuterol — selective β2-adrenergic agonist (example of agonism).
**Chemical antagonism** needs no receptor: positively charged protamine binds and neutralizes negatively charged heparin.
**Physiologic antagonism:** two drugs act on different receptors with opposing effects (e.g., insulin opposes glucocorticoid-induced hyperglycemia).
Classic exam trap: a competitive antagonist shifts the dose-response curve **right** (same Emax, more drug needed); a noncompetitive/irreversible antagonist **lowers the Emax** instead.

A rightward shift with an unchanged plateau is the graphical signature of competitive antagonism — potency falls, but because the antagonism is surmountable, enough agonist can still reach the original Emax.
Inverse agonist ≠ antagonist: only the inverse agonist lowers baseline activity below normal, without any agonist present.
Study-guide distractor: "has no effect on receptor activity whatsoever" matches none of the agonist/antagonist types.

Type: Partial agonist · What it does at the receptor: Submaximal activation · Dose-response curve: Not covered in materials · How to tell apart: Submaximal **even at full occupancy**

Type: Inverse agonist · What it does at the receptor: Reduces baseline (constitutive) activity · Dose-response curve: Not covered in materials · How to tell apart: Lowers activity **below normal with no agonist present**

Type: Competitive antagonist · What it does at the receptor: Reversibly competes at the same site · Dose-response curve: **Shifts right, same Emax** · How to tell apart: Overcome by more agonist (surmountable)

chunks.text: Why can more agonist overcome a competitive antagonist? Both compete **reversibly for the same site** — flood the site with agonist and it wins, so the curve shifts right but the same Emax is still reached.
Why does albuterol open the airways? β2 activation → ↑ intracellular cAMP → bronchial smooth muscle relaxes → bronchodilation.
**C**ompetitive = **C**an be outcompeted (shift right). **N**oncompetitive = **N**o full ceiling (lower Emax).
**Potency:** how much drug is required to produce a given effect — a more potent drug needs a lower dose.
**Efficacy (Emax):** the maximum effect a drug can produce, no matter how high the dose goes.
**EC₅₀:** the drug concentration producing 50% of the maximal effect — the standard measure of potency.
**Therapeutic Index (TI) = TD₅₀ ÷ ED₅₀ (toxic dose in 50% ÷ effective dose in 50%).**
**Quantal dose-response:** ED₅₀ (effective in 50%), TD₅₀ (toxic in 50%), LD₅₀ (lethal in 50% of animals).
**Therapeutic window:** the range between the minimum therapeutic dose and the minimum toxic dose — more practical than TI for dosing a patient.
The sigmoidal dose-response curve: x-axis = log(dose), y-axis = effect. EC₅₀ is on the x-axis; Emax is the plateau — the ceiling effect.
EC₅₀ is read off the curve at the halfway point between baseline and Emax.
Lower EC₅₀ = more potent. Higher Emax = more efficacious.
Potency and efficacy are independent properties — a drug can differ in one without differing in the other.
A curve farther left reaches the same effect at a lower dose (greater potency); curves reaching the same plateau height have identical Emax (efficacy).
A wide TI means a large margin between an effective dose and a toxic dose — generally safer to dose.
A narrow TI means effective and toxic doses are close together — requires careful dosing and often blood-level monitoring.
The distance between the ED₅₀ and TD₅₀ markers is the therapeutic index itself.
Dose-response curves describe potency and efficacy.
Potency clinically matters for dosing — not for choosing the "better" drug.
Efficacy clinically matters much more than potency — a highly potent drug with low efficacy may be clinically useless.
With a narrow TI, a small dosing error can move a patient from effective to toxic — which is why these drugs require blood-level monitoring.
Students should be able to name all four narrow-TI drugs without hesitation and know that each requires therapeutic drug monitoring.
No drug causes only a single specific effect — drugs are **selective**, not specific.
Asthma + hypertension on propranolol: nonselective β blockade can cause bronchoconstriction; a β₁-selective blocker (metoprolol) is an alternative.
**Classic narrow-TI drugs: warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin.**
A drug can be very potent (tiny dose) but have low efficacy — potency alone never tells you whether a drug "works better."
Same Emax + lower dose needed = MORE POTENT, EQUALLY efficacious — not "more efficacious."
EC₅₀ measures potency — not toxicity and not bioavailability.
A narrow-TI drug is not "safer because it needs a lower dose" — it has a smaller margin and needs closer monitoring.
Definition · Potency: How much drug is needed to get an effect · Efficacy (Emax): The maximum effect the drug can produce
Measured by · Potency: EC₅₀ — **lower EC₅₀ = more potent** · Efficacy (Emax): Plateau height — **higher Emax = more efficacious**
On the curve · Potency: Curve farther **left** · Efficacy (Emax): Curve plateaus **higher**
Clinical weight · Potency: Matters for **dosing**, not for picking the "better" drug · Efficacy (Emax): Matters **much more** — potent + low efficacy may be useless
ED₅₀ vs. TD₅₀ · Wide TI: Far apart — large safety margin · Narrow TI: Close together — small safety margin

chunks.text: Why do narrow-TI drugs need blood levels? The effective dose and the toxic dose sit so close together that a small dosing error can push the patient from effective to toxic.
Why does efficacy beat potency clinically? Potency only changes the dose you give; efficacy sets the ceiling of what the drug can achieve at any dose.
Narrow-TI drugs — "**W**atch **L**evels **D**uring **P**rescribing": **W**arfarin, **L**ithium, **D**igoxin, **P**henytoin.
TI = **T**oxic over **E**ffective → TD₅₀ ÷ ED₅₀ (toxic on top).
A — Absorption: movement of drug from the site of administration into the bloodstream.
D — Distribution: movement of drug from blood into tissues.
M — Metabolism: chemical transformation of drug, mainly in the liver.
E — Excretion: removal of drug/metabolites from the body, mainly via the kidney.
**Bioavailability (F) = the fraction of an administered dose that reaches systemic circulation unchanged.**
First-pass effect: the liver metabolizes (can inactivate a large fraction of) an orally absorbed drug before it reaches systemic circulation.
**Volume of distribution (Vd):** a calculated value relating total drug in the body to plasma concentration — a high Vd suggests extensive tissue distribution.
ADME is the organizing skeleton for the rest of the lecture — each remaining pharmacokinetics section is one ADME letter in depth.
ADME determines how much drug reaches its target and for how long.
Metabolism (M arrow → liver) and Excretion (E arrow → kidney) are the back half of ADME — how the body gets rid of the drug; Absorption and Distribution govern how the drug arrives and spreads.
First-pass route: oral drug → GI tract → portal circulation → liver → systemic circulation.
By definition, an IV dose has 100% bioavailability — the entire dose enters the bloodstream directly (no absorption step).
Oral bioavailability is reduced by incomplete absorption and by first-pass hepatic metabolism.
**Plasma protein binding:** only unbound ("free") drug is pharmacologically active and able to cross membranes.
**Lipid solubility:** lipophilic drugs cross membranes more readily and distribute into fatty tissue.
**Tissue perfusion:** highly perfused organs (brain, heart, kidney) receive drug faster than poorly perfused tissue (fat, bone).
Vd is a theoretical volume, not a real anatomic space.
Blood-brain barrier — **Why can some drugs readily enter the CNS while others cannot?** Tight junctions between endothelial cells restrict paracellular movement.
Small, lipophilic, non-ionized drugs cross the BBB more easily than large, polar, or highly protein-bound drugs.
Efflux transporters (like P-glycoprotein) can actively pump some drugs back out of the CNS.
**P-glycoprotein (MDR1)** pumps drugs out of cells in brain, testes, and gut; inhibiting it raises digoxin blood levels.
Ion trapping: weak acids are excreted faster in **alkaline** urine; weak bases faster in **acidic** urine.
Routes that bypass first-pass metabolism: essentially everything except oral — IV, sublingual, inhaled, transdermal, topical, SC, IM.
Sublingual absorption enters systemic venous circulation directly, bypassing the portal vein and the liver's first-pass metabolism; oral dosing passes through the liver first.
Because the liver can inactivate a large fraction of drug first, some drugs are given sublingually or transdermally instead of orally.
A highly polar antibiotic would generally not cross the BBB well — unless the meninges are inflamed, as in meningitis.
Aspirin overdose: sodium bicarbonate alkalinizes blood and urine, reducing aspirin entry into tissues and speeding its renal excretion.
Large first-pass effect: nitroglycerin, propranolol, morphine — all require higher oral doses (or a non-oral route) to achieve the same systemic exposure as IV.
Very high Vd: digoxin — mostly sequestered in tissue, not floating around in plasma.
Subcutaneous route is common for insulin and heparin.
P-glycoprotein — an efflux transporter at the BBB.
IV = 100% bioavailable with no absorption phase; oral is less than 100%.
Taking an oral drug with food or on an empty stomach does not bypass first-pass metabolism — sublingual does.
A very high Vd does not mean a big anatomic space — it means the drug is mostly in tissue, not plasma.
Only free (unbound) drug is active and can cross membranes — protein-bound drug cannot.
Route: Oral (PO) · Key feature: Convenient; subject to first-pass metabolism and variable absorption · Bypasses first-pass?: **No**
Route: Sublingual · Key feature: Absorbed directly into systemic circulation · Bypasses first-pass?: Yes
Route: Intravenous (IV) · Key feature: 100% bioavailable; immediate onset; no absorption phase · Bypasses first-pass?: Yes
Route: Intramuscular (IM) · Key feature: Faster than oral; good for depot/long-acting formulations · Bypasses first-pass?: Yes
Route: Subcutaneous (SC) · Key feature: Slower, steady absorption; common for insulin, heparin · Bypasses first-pass?: Yes
Route: Inhaled · Key feature: Rapid local effect in the lungs; minimizes systemic exposure for some drugs · Bypasses first-pass?: Yes
Route: Transdermal · Key feature: Slow, sustained systemic absorption through the skin · Bypasses first-pass?: Yes
Route: Topical · Key feature: Local effect at the site of application; minimal systemic absorption · Bypasses first-pass?: Yes
Size · Crosses more easily: Small · Crosses less easily: Large

chunks.text: Why is IV bioavailability 100%? The whole dose enters the bloodstream directly — there is no absorption step and no trip through the liver first.
Why does sublingual skip first-pass? It drains into systemic veins, not the portal vein — so the drug reaches the body before the liver can inactivate it.
Why do highly protein-bound drugs act less and cross the BBB poorly? Only free (unbound) drug is active and able to cross membranes.

31.notes: Point to EC50 and Emax directly on the plotted curve — this is the same curve concept described on the previous slide, now shown graphically.

34.title: Potency vs. Efficacy
34.notes: Classic PA-exam framing: a drug can be very potent (tiny dose) but have low efficacy — potency alone never tells you whether a drug "works better."

35.title: Potency vs. Efficacy, Side by Side
35.notes: Left panel: two drugs with the same Emax but different EC50 (potency differs). Right panel: two drugs with the same EC50 but different Emax (efficacy differs). This is the graphical version of the table on the previous slide.

38.title: The Therapeutic Index
38.notes: These four narrow-TI drugs are extremely high-yield — students should be able to name all four without hesitation and know that each requires therapeutic drug monitoring.

39.title: Wide vs. Narrow Therapeutic Index
39.notes: Point out how close ED50 and TD50 sit for the narrow-TI example — this is exactly why warfarin, lithium, digoxin, and phenytoin require blood-level monitoring.

45.title: ADME
45.notes: Tell students ADME is the organizing skeleton for the rest of this lecture — each remaining pharmacokinetics section is really just one ADME letter in depth.

46.title: The ADME Compartment Model
46.notes: Trace the arrows A-D-M-E with your finger as you narrate — this is the visual skeleton for the rest of the ADME discussion (and for the remaining PK sections in Session 2).

49.title: Routes of Administration
49.notes: Ask students which routes bypass first-pass metabolism (IV, sublingual, inhaled, transdermal, topical, SC, IM — essentially everything except oral).

50.title: Bioavailability
50.notes: This naturally sets up the next slide on first-pass metabolism as the main reason oral bioavailability is less than 100%.

51.title: The First-Pass Effect
51.notes: The liver can inactivate a large fraction of drug before it ever reaches systemic circulation — this is why some drugs are given sublingually or transdermally instead of orally.

52.title: Distribution
52.notes: Vd is a theoretical volume, not a real anatomic space — a drug with a very high Vd (like digoxin) is telling you it is mostly sequestered in tissue, not floating around in plasma.

53.title: The Blood-Brain Barrier
53.notes: Use this as a think-pair-share — ask students to predict whether a highly polar antibiotic would cross the BBB well (generally no, unless meninges are inflamed, as in meningitis).

U1-R1.question: Define pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics in one sentence each. Which one is "what the body does to the drug," and which is "what the drug does to the body"?
U1-R1.answer: PK = what the body does to the drug (ADME); PD = what the drug does to the body (receptors/effect).

U1-R2.question: Why do PAs default to prescribing and counseling patients using a drug's generic name rather than its brand name?
U1-R2.answer: Generic names are unambiguous and international, preventing confusion when the same ingredient hides under multiple brand names (e.g., acetaminophen/Tylenol), which can cause unintentional double-dosing.

U1-R3.question: List the four clinical trial phases in order and state the primary purpose and typical study population of each.
U1-R3.answer: Phase I — safety/dosing in healthy volunteers; Phase II — preliminary efficacy in a few hundred patients; Phase III — confirm efficacy/monitor safety at scale; Phase IV — postmarketing surveillance.

U1-R4.question: Define efficacy and effectiveness. Why might a drug with strong trial efficacy still underperform in everyday practice?
U1-R4.answer: Efficacy = performance under ideal trial conditions; effectiveness = performance in real-world practice (adherence, comorbidities, interactions can all reduce effectiveness below trial efficacy).

U1-R5.question: Name the five major drug target classes drugs can act on.
U1-R5.answer: Receptors, ion channels, enzymes, transporters, nucleic acids.

U1-R6.question: Define potency and efficacy (Emax). If Drug X needs a lower dose than Drug Y to produce the same effect, but both reach the same Emax, which drug is more potent, and which is more efficacious?
U1-R6.answer: Potency = dose needed for an effect (lower EC50 = more potent); efficacy = maximum achievable effect (Emax). Drug X is more potent; both are equally efficacious.

U1-R7.question: Write the formula for Therapeutic Index (TI). What does a narrow TI mean for how a drug must be dosed and monitored? Name two classic narrow-TI drugs.
U1-R7.answer: TI = TD50 ÷ ED50; narrow TI requires careful dosing and often blood-level monitoring; warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin.

U1-R8.question: Define bioavailability (F). Why is an IV dose's bioavailability always 100%?
U1-R8.answer: F = fraction of dose reaching systemic circulation unchanged; IV is 100% because there is no absorption step.

U1-R9.question: What is the first-pass effect? Name two drugs significantly affected by it, and explain why sublingual or IV dosing avoids it.
U1-R9.answer: Hepatic metabolism of an orally absorbed drug before it reaches systemic circulation; nitroglycerin, propranolol, morphine; sublingual/IV bypass the portal vein and liver.

quiz.stem: A patient says they take no medications, but separately mentions using "Tylenol" for headaches and a combination cold-and-flu product. What does this scenario illustrate?

options.A: Brand names can obscure a shared generic ingredient, risking unintentional double-dosing
options.B: Chemical names are standardized internationally, so this mix-up could not happen
options.C: Generic names vary by manufacturer, which caused the confusion
options.D: Pharmacologic effect and therapeutic effect are simply two words for the same thing

quiz.why: Different brand-name products (Tylenol, many combination cold/flu products) can share the same active generic ingredient. Prescribing and counseling by generic name avoids hiding duplicate therapy — the reason PAs default to generic names.
quiz.label: Lecture check 1 · S8-9

quiz.stem: In which clinical trial phase is a drug first tested in a large patient population specifically to confirm efficacy and monitor for adverse effects at scale, just before approval?

options.A: Phase I
options.B: Phase II
options.C: Phase III
options.D: Phase IV

quiz.why: Phase III trials enroll hundreds to thousands of patients, often at multiple sites, to confirm efficacy and monitor safety at scale before approval. Phase I is small-scale safety/dosing, Phase II is preliminary efficacy, and Phase IV is postmarketing surveillance after approval.
quiz.label: Lecture check 2 · S16-17

quiz.stem: In Figure 1 above, the dashed curve (+ Competitive antagonist) is shifted to the right of the agonist-alone curve but reaches the same plateau at the top. What does this pattern show?

options.A: More agonist is needed to reach the same effect, but the same maximal effect is still achievable
options.B: The competitive antagonist lowers the drug’s efficacy (Emax)
options.C: The competitive antagonist increases the drug’s potency
options.D: The competitive antagonist has no measurable effect on the agonist’s curve

quiz.why: A rightward shift with an unchanged plateau is the graphical signature of competitive antagonism: it takes more drug to reach a given effect (potency falls), but because the antagonism is surmountable, enough agonist can still reach the original Emax. Contrast this with the noncompetitive/irreversible curve in the same figure, which plateaus lower instead of shifting right.
quiz.label: Lecture check 3 · S24-25

quiz.stem: A drug binds the same receptor as an endogenous agonist and lowers the tissue’s baseline (constitutive) activity below normal, without any agonist present. This drug is best classified as a(n):

options.A: Full agonist
options.B: Partial agonist
options.C: Competitive antagonist
options.D: Inverse agonist

quiz.why: An inverse agonist actively reduces constitutive (baseline) receptor activity below normal — a true antagonist merely blocks the agonist without lowering baseline activity itself.
quiz.label: Lecture check 4 · S27-28

quiz.stem: On the dose-response curve in Figure 2, the point marked EC₅₀ sits exactly halfway up the rising part of the curve. What does this point represent?

options.A: The dose at which the drug becomes toxic
options.B: The concentration producing 50% of the drug’s maximal effect
options.C: The point where the drug has zero effect
options.D: The drug’s bioavailability

quiz.why: EC₅₀ is read directly off the curve at the halfway point between baseline and Emax (the plateau) — it is the standard graphical measure of potency, not a measure of toxicity or bioavailability.
quiz.label: Lecture check 5 · S32-33

quiz.stem: In the left panel of Figure 3, Drug A’s curve sits to the left of Drug B’s curve, but both curves plateau at the same height. What does this tell you?

options.A: Drug A is more potent than Drug B, and both have equal efficacy
options.B: Drug A is more efficacious than Drug B
options.C: Drug A and Drug B have different Emax values
options.D: Drug B is more potent than Drug A

quiz.why: A curve positioned farther left reaches the same effect at a lower dose — that is greater potency. Because both curves reach the same plateau height, their Emax (efficacy) is identical; only potency differs, exactly as the right panel then shows the reverse case (same potency, different efficacy).
quiz.label: Lecture check 6 · S36-37

quiz.stem: Comparing the two number lines in Figure 4, the narrow-TI drug’s ED₅₀ and TD₅₀ markers sit much closer together than the wide-TI drug’s. What is the clinical implication?

options.A: The narrow-TI drug is safer because it requires a lower dose
options.B: The narrow-TI drug has a smaller margin between an effective and a toxic dose, requiring closer monitoring
options.C: The wide-TI drug is more likely to cause toxicity
options.D: Therapeutic index has no bearing on dosing safety

quiz.why: The distance between the ED₅₀ and TD₅₀ markers on the number line is the therapeutic index itself — a narrow gap (as with warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin) means a small dosing error can move a patient from effective to toxic, which is why these drugs require blood-level monitoring.
quiz.label: Lecture check 7 · S40-41

quiz.stem: Drug X requires a much lower dose than Drug Y to achieve the same effect, but both drugs achieve the same maximum effect (Emax). Which statement is correct?

options.A: Drug X is more efficacious than Drug Y
options.B: Drug X is more potent than Drug Y
options.C: Drug X has a narrower therapeutic index than Drug Y
options.D: Drug X and Drug Y have different Emax values

quiz.why: Needing a lower dose for the same effect is the definition of greater potency. Since both drugs reach the same Emax, their efficacy is equal — potency and efficacy are independent properties.
quiz.label: Lecture check 8 · S42-43

quiz.stem: In Figure 5, two separate arrows leave the Central Compartment box: one labeled "M" pointing to Metabolism (Liver), and one labeled "E" pointing to Excretion (Kidney). Together, these two arrows represent which part of ADME?

options.A: Absorption and Distribution
options.B: Distribution only
options.C: Metabolism and Excretion — how the drug is transformed and cleared
options.D: Only the Excretion step

quiz.why: The diagram shows drug leaving the Central Compartment by two separate routes: the "M" arrow to the liver (biotransformation) and the "E" arrow to the kidney (elimination). Together these are the back half of ADME — how the body gets rid of the drug, as opposed to Absorption and Distribution, which govern how the drug arrives and spreads.
quiz.label: Lecture check 9 · S47-48

quiz.stem: Which route of administration bypasses first-pass hepatic metabolism entirely, by entering systemic venous circulation directly?

options.A: Sublingual
options.B: Oral, taken on an empty stomach
options.C: All routes undergo first-pass metabolism equally
options.D: Oral, taken with food

quiz.why: Sublingual absorption enters systemic venous circulation directly, bypassing the portal vein and the liver’s first-pass metabolism — unlike oral dosing, which is absorbed into the portal circulation and passes through the liver first.
quiz.label: Lecture check 10 · S54-55

quiz.stem: A 45-year-old patient takes a new medication exactly as prescribed. Drug levels are within the therapeutic range, yet the patient develops an unintended, harmful response. Which term best describes this event?

options.A: Toxicity, because any harmful drug response counts as toxicity
options.B: A therapeutic effect, because the drug was taken exactly as prescribed
options.C: An adverse drug reaction, because it occurred at a normal therapeutic dose
options.D: A pharmacologic effect only, because it was a measurable biological change
options.E: Irreversible antagonism, because the receptor was permanently inactivated

quiz.why: An ADR is an unintended and harmful response occurring at normal therapeutic doses (S5).

whys.A: Toxicity is harm that occurs as dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range (S5); here levels were within range.
whys.B: A therapeutic effect is the intended, beneficial effect (S5); this response was unintended and harmful.
whys.C: An ADR is an unintended and harmful response occurring at normal therapeutic doses (S5).
whys.D: Every ADR is a pharmacologic effect, but 'unintended and harmful at normal doses' is the more specific, best answer (S5).
whys.E: Irreversible antagonism describes receptor inactivation until new receptor is synthesized (S22) — not a type of adverse event.

quiz.label: Q1 · Clinical vignette · The Language of Pharmacology

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes pharmacokinetics from pharmacodynamics?

options.A: Pharmacokinetics studies receptor binding; pharmacodynamics studies absorption and excretion
options.B: Pharmacokinetics applies only to IV drugs; pharmacodynamics applies only to oral drugs
options.C: Pharmacokinetics studies genetic variation; pharmacodynamics studies poisoning and overdose
options.D: Pharmacokinetics is what the drug does to the body; pharmacodynamics is what the body does to the drug
options.E: Pharmacokinetics is what the body does to the drug; pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to the body

quiz.why: PK = what the body does to the drug (ADME); PD = what the drug does to the body (receptors & effect) (S6).

whys.A: Receptors & effect belong to PD; absorption and excretion (ADME) belong to PK (S6).
whys.B: Neither branch is defined by route; PK covers ADME for any route (S6, S49).
whys.C: Genetic variation = pharmacogenomics; poisoning = clinical pharmacology/toxicology (S6).
whys.E: PK = what the body does to the drug (ADME); PD = what the drug does to the body (receptors & effect) (S6).

quiz.label: Q2 · Mechanism · The Language of Pharmacology

quiz.stem: A drug relieved symptoms in most participants of a controlled multi-site trial. In your clinic, far fewer patients improve; many miss doses and have several comorbidities. Which concept best explains the gap?

options.A: A narrow therapeutic index that appeared after approval
options.B: Real-world effectiveness falling below the drug's trial efficacy
options.C: Lower potency than was measured during trial dose-finding
options.D: Extensive first-pass metabolism in the clinic's patients
options.E: Competitive antagonism of the drug by the comorbid conditions

quiz.why: Efficacy is performance under ideal trial conditions; effectiveness is performance in everyday practice with real-world adherence and comorbidities (S14).

whys.A: TI describes the gap between effective and toxic doses (S38), not missed doses or comorbidities.
whys.B: Efficacy is performance under ideal trial conditions; effectiveness is performance in everyday practice with real-world adherence and comorbidities (S14).
whys.C: Potency is the dose needed for an effect and matters for dosing, not for whether patients improve (S34).
whys.D: First-pass effect lowers oral bioavailability (S50-51); it doesn't explain adherence- and comorbidity-driven differences.
whys.E: Competitive antagonism is a drug competing at the same receptor site (S22), not a disease effect.

quiz.label: Q3 · Clinical vignette · Drug Development & Regulation

quiz.stem: Two years after approval, reports reveal a serious reaction occurring in about 1 in 10,000 patients — never seen in the clinical trials. Which best explains why it was missed before approval?

options.A: Adverse-event reporting systems accept only voluntary reports
options.B: Approval came before the drug completed any clinical trial phase
options.C: Trial populations were too small and too short to detect so rare an event
options.D: Phase I trials enrolled patients who already had the target condition
options.E: Phase III trials are not designed to monitor adverse effects

quiz.why: Rare adverse effects are often first detected in Phase IV because trial populations are too small and too short in duration to catch 1-in-10,000 events (S12 notes).

whys.A: Reporting systems are both voluntary and mandatory (S14).
whys.B: Approved drugs pass through a structured pipeline with clinical trials before FDA review (S12, S56).
whys.C: Rare adverse effects are often first detected in Phase IV because trial populations are too small and too short in duration to catch 1-in-10,000 events (S12 notes).
whys.D: Phase I uses a small group of healthy volunteers (S13).
whys.E: Phase III confirms efficacy AND monitors adverse effects at scale (S13).

quiz.label: Q4 · Clinical vignette · Drug Development & Regulation

quiz.stem: According to the textbook, which clinical trial phase has the highest rate of drug failures?

options.A: Phase IV
options.B: Phase II
options.C: FDA review
options.D: Phase III

quiz.why: Phase II has the highest failure rate; only about 25% of drugs move on to Phase III (p. 17).

whys.A: Phase IV is postmarketing surveillance after approval (p. 17).
whys.B: Phase II has the highest failure rate; only about 25% of drugs move on to Phase III (p. 17).
whys.C: FDA review is the approval step after Phase III, not a trial phase (p. 17).
whys.D: Phase III confirms efficacy in thousands, after most failures have occurred (p. 17).
whys.E: Phase I sets the safe dose range in 20–100 subjects; it is not the main failure point (p. 17).

quiz.label: Q5 · Mechanism · Drug Development & Regulation

quiz.stem: A 22-year-old patient inhales albuterol, and within minutes the bronchial smooth muscle relaxes. Which sequence best explains this effect?

options.A: β2 receptor blockade → falling intracellular cAMP → smooth muscle relaxation
options.B: Enzyme inhibition → falling intracellular cAMP → bronchial smooth muscle dilation
options.C: Ion channel opening → rising intracellular cAMP → smooth muscle contraction
options.D: β2 receptor activation → rising intracellular cAMP → smooth muscle relaxation
options.E: Inverse agonism at β2 → lowered baseline activity → smooth muscle relaxation

quiz.why: Albuterol is a selective β2 agonist: binding activates β2 → increases cAMP → relaxes bronchial smooth muscle → bronchodilation (S26).

whys.A: Albuterol is an agonist — it activates, not blocks, β2, and cAMP rises (S26).
whys.B: The mechanism is receptor activation with rising cAMP (S26).
whys.C: Albuterol acts on the β2 receptor, and the result is relaxation, not contraction (S26).
whys.D: Albuterol is a selective β2 agonist: binding activates β2 → increases cAMP → relaxes bronchial smooth muscle → bronchodilation (S26).
whys.E: Inverse agonists reduce baseline activity (S22); albuterol is a selective β2 agonist (S26).

quiz.label: Q6 · Clinical vignette · Pharmacodynamics: Targets & Receptors

quiz.stem: A patient receives a drug that blocks a receptor. Raising the dose of the agonist medication eventually restores the full original maximal response. The blocking drug is most likely a(n):

options.A: Noncompetitive antagonist
options.B: Competitive antagonist
options.C: Inverse agonist
options.D: Irreversible antagonist

quiz.why: A competitive antagonist reversibly competes at the same site and is overcome by more agonist — same Emax, curve shifted right (S22, S22 notes).

whys.A: Noncompetitive antagonists reduce the maximal effect, so full Emax is not restored (S22).
whys.B: A competitive antagonist reversibly competes at the same site and is overcome by more agonist — same Emax, curve shifted right (S22, S22 notes).
whys.C: An inverse agonist lowers baseline activity; the scenario describes surmountable blockade (S22, S28).
whys.D: Irreversible antagonists permanently inactivate receptors until new ones are synthesized, lowering Emax (S22, S22 notes).
whys.E: A partial agonist itself gives submaximal activation (S22); it is not described as a blocker overcome by more agonist.

quiz.label: Q7 · Mechanism · Pharmacodynamics: Targets & Receptors

quiz.stem: A 54-year-old is given phenoxybenzamine before surgery for pheochromocytoma. Blood pressure stays controlled even when the tumor releases large catecholamine surges. What best explains why the blockade persists?

options.A: It activates opposing receptors, producing a physiologic counter-effect instead
options.B: It is a partial agonist that caps the maximal catecholamine response
options.C: It neutralizes catecholamines chemically in plasma before they reach receptors
options.D: It competes reversibly, so high catecholamine levels easily displace it
options.E: It binds receptors irreversibly; effect lasts until new receptors are made

quiz.why: An irreversible antagonist's duration depends on receptor turnover, and high agonist levels cannot overcome it (p. 25).

whys.A: That is physiologic antagonism, like insulin vs glucocorticoids (p. 27).
whys.B: Partial agonists produce a submaximal response; phenoxybenzamine is an irreversible antagonist (p. 25; p. 26).
whys.C: That is chemical antagonism, like protamine–heparin (p. 26).
whys.D: That describes competitive antagonism, which surges CAN overcome (p. 25).
whys.E: An irreversible antagonist's duration depends on receptor turnover, and high agonist levels cannot overcome it (p. 25).

quiz.label: Q8 · Clinical vignette · Pharmacodynamics: Targets & Receptors

quiz.stem: A PA is starting a patient on lithium. Compared with a drug that has a wide therapeutic index, what does lithium's narrow therapeutic index mean for this patient's care?

options.A: Lithium is more potent, so it can be dosed without monitoring levels
options.B: Lithium has a large safety margin, so dosing errors are well tolerated
options.C: Effective and toxic doses are close, so dose carefully and monitor blood levels
options.D: Lithium has a higher Emax, so lower doses than usual are always enough
options.E: Lithium is 100% bioavailable, so blood levels never need to be checked

quiz.why: A narrow TI means effective and toxic doses are close together — requiring careful dosing and often blood-level monitoring; lithium is a classic narrow-TI drug (S38).

whys.A: Potency matters for dosing amount, not safety margin; narrow-TI drugs need monitoring (S34, S38).
whys.C: A narrow TI means effective and toxic doses are close together — requiring careful dosing and often blood-level monitoring; lithium is a classic narrow-TI drug (S38).
whys.D: TI is about toxic vs. effective doses, not Emax (S30, S38).
whys.E: Bioavailability is a different concept (S50); narrow-TI drugs need monitoring (S38).

quiz.label: Q9 · Clinical vignette · Dose-Response Relationships

quiz.stem: Two drugs relieve the same symptom. Drug A works at 5 mg and Drug B at 50 mg, but at maximal doses Drug B produces a much greater maximal effect. Which statement best guides drug selection?

options.A: Drug B has greater potency because its maximal effect is much higher
options.B: Both drugs have equal efficacy because both relieve the same symptom
options.C: Drug A has greater efficacy because it needs a much smaller dose
options.D: Drug B has greater efficacy, which matters more clinically than Drug A's potency
options.E: Drug A should be chosen because greater potency means it works better

quiz.why: Efficacy (Emax) clinically matters much more than potency — a highly potent drug with low efficacy may be clinically useless (S34).

whys.A: Higher Emax = more efficacious, not more potent (S34).
whys.B: Drug B reaches a higher maximal effect, so its efficacy is greater (S30).
whys.C: A smaller dose means greater POTENCY; efficacy is the maximum effect (S30).
whys.D: Efficacy (Emax) clinically matters much more than potency — a highly potent drug with low efficacy may be clinically useless (S34).
whys.E: Potency alone never tells you whether a drug works better (S34 notes).

quiz.label: Q10 · Clinical vignette · Dose-Response Relationships

quiz.stem: A patient stable on IV propranolol is switched to the oral form and needs a much higher oral dose to reach the same systemic exposure. Which best explains this?

options.A: Oral propranolol cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, so more must be given
options.B: Propranolol has a narrow therapeutic index, so oral doses must be higher
options.C: The IV form was less than 100% bioavailable, so less drug reached the blood
options.D: Propranolol is highly protein-bound, so the oral form is inactive in plasma
options.E: Extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism lowers the drug's oral bioavailability

quiz.why: Propranolol has a large first-pass effect; oral doses pass GI → portal → liver before systemic circulation, so higher oral doses are needed to match IV exposure (S51, S50).

whys.A: BBB crossing relates to CNS entry (S53), not systemic exposure after an oral dose.
whys.B: Narrow TI calls for careful dosing and monitoring (S38); propranolol is named for first-pass, not narrow TI (S51).
whys.D: Protein binding affects free drug in plasma regardless of route (S52); the IV-to-oral gap is the first-pass effect (S51).
whys.E: Propranolol has a large first-pass effect; oral doses pass GI → portal → liver before systemic circulation, so higher oral doses are needed to match IV exposure (S51, S50).

quiz.label: Q11 · Clinical vignette · Pharmacokinetics: ADME — Absorption & Distribution

quiz.stem: A patient with meningitis receives a highly polar antibiotic. Which statement best describes this drug's ability to reach the CNS?

options.A: Polar drugs usually cross poorly, but inflamed meninges allow better entry
options.B: Polar drugs never reach the CNS, even when the meninges are inflamed
options.C: Polar drugs cross easily because P-glycoprotein pumps them into the CNS
options.D: Polar drugs cross easily because tight junctions favor polar molecules

children.name: Key definitions
facts: **Pharmacology:** the scientific study of how drugs interact with living systems — from the molecular level to the whole patient.
**Drug (medication):** any chemical substance used to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent disease, or to alter a physiologic process.
**Pharmacologic effect:** a measurable biological change a drug produces (e.g., lower blood pressure).
**Therapeutic effect:** the intended, beneficial pharmacologic effect for a given condition.
**Adverse drug reaction (ADR):** an unintended and harmful response occurring at normal therapeutic doses.
**Toxicity:** harmful effects that occur as the dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.
**Chemical name:** describes the exact molecular structure (rarely used in clinical practice).
**Generic name:** the official, non-proprietary name assigned to the active drug — one generic name per drug, regardless of manufacturer.
**Brand (trade) name:** the manufacturer's marketed name; the same generic drug may have several brand names, and brand names change between countries.
**Prodrug:** an inactive precursor converted to the active drug in the body (usually by metabolism).
**Poisons** are drugs with almost exclusively harmful effects — but "the dose makes the poison" (Paracelsus): any substance can harm at the wrong dose.

children.name: How it works
facts: Pharmacokinetics = what the body does to the drug — ADME.
Pharmacodynamics = what the drug does to the body — receptors & effect.
Pharmacogenomics = how genetic variation shapes individual drug response.
Clinical Pharmacology / Toxicology = applying PK/PD to real patients, and the study of poisoning.
This map covers the whole lecture: PK and PD are the two biggest buckets, and nearly everything else (toxicology, pharmacogenomics, therapeutics) sits on top of them.

children.name: Clinical relevance
facts: **PA students should learn and prescribe by generic name — it is unambiguous, international, and avoids confusing a patient's multiple brand-name products for different drugs.**
Different brand-name products (Tylenol, many combination cold/flu products) can share the same active generic ingredient.
Prescribing and counseling by generic name avoids hiding duplicate therapy — the reason PAs default to generic names.
If a patient says they take "Tylenol" and separately "acetaminophen," check for accidental double-dosing — this previews the acetaminophen toxicity discussion.
Precise vocabulary (generic names, therapeutic vs. adverse effects) protects patients.
More than half of prescriptions in the USA are for generic drugs.

children.name: Drugs named as examples
facts: Acetaminophen (generic) is sold as Tylenol and under many store brands.

children.name: Exam traps
facts: "Therapeutic effect" and "pharmacologic effect" are not synonyms — a drug can have pharmacologic effects that are not therapeutic (that is often exactly what an adverse effect is).
ADR vs. toxicity: an ADR happens at normal therapeutic doses; toxicity happens when dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.
Generic names do NOT vary by manufacturer (one per drug); brand names DO vary — and change between countries.

children.name: Key definitions
facts: **Efficacy:** how well a drug works under ideal, controlled trial conditions.
**Effectiveness:** how well a drug works in everyday clinical practice, with real-world adherence and comorbidities.
Drug interactions can also reduce real-world effectiveness below trial efficacy.
**Benefit vs. risk:** the central question regulators and prescribers must weigh for every approval and every prescription.
**Adverse-event reporting:** ongoing, voluntary and mandatory reporting systems (e.g., FDA MedWatch) that catch safety signals after approval.

children.name: How it works
facts: Where new drugs come from — Natural products: plants, fungi, microbes, marine organisms.
Synthetic & biotech: designed small molecules; recombinant proteins.
Biologics: monoclonal antibodies, gene- and cell-based therapies.
Drug repurposing: an existing approved drug found to treat a new condition.
From discovery to patient: Discovery → Preclinical testing → Clinical trials → FDA review → Approval → Postmarket surveillance.
Most candidate drugs fail somewhere along this pipeline — approval is the exception, not the rule.
Phase I: safety, tolerability, dose-finding — a small group of healthy volunteers.
Phase II: preliminary efficacy and side-effect profile — a few hundred patients with the target condition.
Phase III: confirm efficacy and monitor adverse effects at scale — hundreds to thousands of patients, often multi-site.
Phase IV: postmarketing surveillance after approval — the general prescribed population.
Every approved drug has passed through a structured development and regulatory pipeline (Phases I–IV).
Phase II has the **highest failure rate** — only about 25% of new drugs move on to Phase III.
Phase III usually enrolls **thousands** of patients (Figure 1–6: 1000–6000), often double-blind and crossover, in settings like the drug's eventual use.
Less than one-third of drugs studied in humans survive clinical trials and reach the market.
To see one case of a toxicity occurring 1 in 10,000, several hundred thousand patients may need exposure — so rare effects usually surface only in Phase IV, which has **no fixed duration**.
Marketing requires a **New Drug Application (NDA)** after Phase III; human testing starts only after an **IND** (Investigational New Drug) application.

children.name: Clinical relevance
facts: Postmarketing surveillance (Phase IV) is where rare adverse effects are often first detected — trial populations are too small and too short in duration to catch 1-in-10,000 events.

Case: a new medication improves symptoms in 70% of patients with a chronic, non-life-threatening condition, but postmarketing data show serious hepatotoxicity in about 1%. **Would you prescribe it — and does your answer depend on what else is available?**

**Clinical pearl:** risk-benefit analysis is always comparative — a 1% serious-toxicity rate reads very differently if it is the only effective option versus if three safer alternatives already exist.
Ask "compared to what?" rather than judging the number in isolation.
A patent lasts 20 years; after it expires, generics are approved through an **abbreviated new drug application (ANDA)** that requires bioequivalence data.
Placebo responses can occur in as many as 30–40% of subjects — the reason controlled, blinded trials are needed.
Adverse events that are both **serious and unexpected** must be reported to the FDA within 15 days; clinicians can report through MedWatch.

children.name: Drugs named as examples
facts: FDA MedWatch — an adverse-event reporting system.
Biologic DMARDs (MSK unit, later) are a direct example of the "biotechnology" drug source.
**Thalidomide** (sold in Europe as a "nontoxic" hypnotic) caused about 10,000 birth defects and led to the **Kefauver-Harris Amendments (1962)**, which required proof of efficacy as well as safety.
The **Orphan Drug Amendment (1983)** gives incentives for drugs treating diseases with fewer than 200,000 US patients.

children.name: Exam traps
facts: Efficacy vs. effectiveness is a favorite exam distinction: efficacy is the trial result; effectiveness is what happens once real patients with real adherence patterns use the drug.
Phase III — not Phase I, II, or IV — is the large pre-approval trial that confirms efficacy and monitors safety at scale.
Phase III is what most people picture as "the" clinical trial, but regulatory decisions already begin shaping the drug long before that.

children.name: Key definitions
facts: **Drug target:** the specific molecule a drug binds to produce its effect.
**Receptor:** a protein target whose activation (or blockade) triggers a cellular response.
**Signal transduction:** the chain of molecular events that converts receptor binding into a cellular effect.
**Pharmacologic response:** the measurable downstream result — contraction, secretion, gene transcription, and so on.
Full agonist — maximal receptor activation.
Partial agonist — submaximal activation, even at full receptor occupancy.
Inverse agonist — reduces baseline (constitutive) receptor activity.
Competitive antagonist — reversibly competes with agonist at the same site; overcome by more agonist.
Noncompetitive antagonist — binds elsewhere or irreversibly reduces the maximal effect.
Irreversible antagonist — permanently inactivates the receptor until new receptor is synthesized.

children.name: How it works
facts: The pathway: drug → target → signal transduction → response. Every pharmacodynamics topic for the rest of the course maps onto this chain.
Receptor concept: Drug + Receptor → Drug-Receptor Complex → Cellular Response.
This single chain underlies agonism, antagonism, potency, and efficacy — all describe different features of this interaction.
Five major drug target classes: receptors, ion channels, enzymes, transporters, nucleic acids.
Receptors: G-protein-coupled, ligand-gated ion channel, enzyme-linked, nuclear.
Ion channels: directly gate the flow of ions across a membrane.
Enzymes: drugs can inhibit or, less commonly, activate an enzyme's activity.
Transporters & nucleic acids: carrier proteins; or DNA/RNA for some antimicrobials & gene therapies.
Most drugs target receptors or enzymes — ion channels and transporters matter especially for cardiac and CNS drugs.
An inverse agonist actively reduces constitutive (baseline) receptor activity below normal; a true antagonist merely blocks the agonist without lowering baseline activity itself.
**Spare receptors:** a maximal response can occur without occupying every receptor (e.g., about 90% of cardiac β receptors can be blocked and maximal inotropic response still preserved).
**Irreversible antagonist** effects last until new receptors are made — duration depends on receptor turnover, not drug elimination (phenoxybenzamine for pheochromocytoma).
A partial agonist's lower maximal effect is **not** due to lower affinity — it can occupy all receptors and still produce less response.
**Allosteric modulators** bind a different site from the agonist (e.g., benzodiazepines enhance GABA's effect).
Agonist-induced **desensitization** (tachyphylaxis) and downregulation reduce response with continued exposure.

children.name: Clinical relevance
facts: Albuterol is a selective β2-adrenergic receptor agonist.
Binding activates the β2 receptor → increases intracellular cAMP.
Rising cAMP relaxes bronchial smooth muscle → bronchodilation.
**This is the same receptor-to-response logic you will reuse for every agonist drug this term.**
Albuterol bridges introductory pharmacodynamics into the pulmonary pharmacology seen later in the curriculum.
Competitive antagonism is surmountable in real life: exercise or stress raises catecholamines enough to overcome a fixed propranolol dose.
Propranolol markedly slows the heart rate in pheochromocytoma (high catecholamines) but not the resting rate of a trained marathon runner.

children.name: Drugs named as examples
facts: Albuterol — selective β2-adrenergic agonist (example of agonism).
**Chemical antagonism** needs no receptor: positively charged protamine binds and neutralizes negatively charged heparin.
**Physiologic antagonism:** two drugs act on different receptors with opposing effects (e.g., insulin opposes glucocorticoid-induced hyperglycemia).

children.name: Exam traps
facts: Classic exam trap: a competitive antagonist shifts the dose-response curve **right** (same Emax, more drug needed); a noncompetitive/irreversible antagonist **lowers the Emax** instead.

A rightward shift with an unchanged plateau is the graphical signature of competitive antagonism — potency falls, but because the antagonism is surmountable, enough agonist can still reach the original Emax.
Inverse agonist ≠ antagonist: only the inverse agonist lowers baseline activity below normal, without any agonist present.
Study-guide distractor: "has no effect on receptor activity whatsoever" matches none of the agonist/antagonist types.

children.name: Key definitions
facts: **Potency:** how much drug is required to produce a given effect — a more potent drug needs a lower dose.
**Efficacy (Emax):** the maximum effect a drug can produce, no matter how high the dose goes.
**EC₅₀:** the drug concentration producing 50% of the maximal effect — the standard measure of potency.
**Therapeutic Index (TI) = TD₅₀ ÷ ED₅₀ (toxic dose in 50% ÷ effective dose in 50%).**
**Quantal dose-response:** ED₅₀ (effective in 50%), TD₅₀ (toxic in 50%), LD₅₀ (lethal in 50% of animals).
**Therapeutic window:** the range between the minimum therapeutic dose and the minimum toxic dose — more practical than TI for dosing a patient.

children.name: How it works
facts: The sigmoidal dose-response curve: x-axis = log(dose), y-axis = effect. EC₅₀ is on the x-axis; Emax is the plateau — the ceiling effect.
EC₅₀ is read off the curve at the halfway point between baseline and Emax.
Lower EC₅₀ = more potent. Higher Emax = more efficacious.
Potency and efficacy are independent properties — a drug can differ in one without differing in the other.
A curve farther left reaches the same effect at a lower dose (greater potency); curves reaching the same plateau height have identical Emax (efficacy).
A wide TI means a large margin between an effective dose and a toxic dose — generally safer to dose.
A narrow TI means effective and toxic doses are close together — requires careful dosing and often blood-level monitoring.
The distance between the ED₅₀ and TD₅₀ markers is the therapeutic index itself.
Dose-response curves describe potency and efficacy.

children.name: Clinical relevance
facts: Potency clinically matters for dosing — not for choosing the "better" drug.
Efficacy clinically matters much more than potency — a highly potent drug with low efficacy may be clinically useless.
With a narrow TI, a small dosing error can move a patient from effective to toxic — which is why these drugs require blood-level monitoring.
Students should be able to name all four narrow-TI drugs without hesitation and know that each requires therapeutic drug monitoring.
No drug causes only a single specific effect — drugs are **selective**, not specific.
Asthma + hypertension on propranolol: nonselective β blockade can cause bronchoconstriction; a β₁-selective blocker (metoprolol) is an alternative.

children.name: Drugs named as examples
facts: **Classic narrow-TI drugs: warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin.**

children.name: Exam traps
facts: A drug can be very potent (tiny dose) but have low efficacy — potency alone never tells you whether a drug "works better."
Same Emax + lower dose needed = MORE POTENT, EQUALLY efficacious — not "more efficacious."
EC₅₀ measures potency — not toxicity and not bioavailability.
A narrow-TI drug is not "safer because it needs a lower dose" — it has a smaller margin and needs closer monitoring.

children.name: Key definitions
facts: A — Absorption: movement of drug from the site of administration into the bloodstream.
D — Distribution: movement of drug from blood into tissues.
M — Metabolism: chemical transformation of drug, mainly in the liver.
E — Excretion: removal of drug/metabolites from the body, mainly via the kidney.
**Bioavailability (F) = the fraction of an administered dose that reaches systemic circulation unchanged.**
First-pass effect: the liver metabolizes (can inactivate a large fraction of) an orally absorbed drug before it reaches systemic circulation.
**Volume of distribution (Vd):** a calculated value relating total drug in the body to plasma concentration — a high Vd suggests extensive tissue distribution.

children.name: How it works
facts: ADME is the organizing skeleton for the rest of the lecture — each remaining pharmacokinetics section is one ADME letter in depth.
ADME determines how much drug reaches its target and for how long.
Metabolism (M arrow → liver) and Excretion (E arrow → kidney) are the back half of ADME — how the body gets rid of the drug; Absorption and Distribution govern how the drug arrives and spreads.
First-pass route: oral drug → GI tract → portal circulation → liver → systemic circulation.
By definition, an IV dose has 100% bioavailability — the entire dose enters the bloodstream directly (no absorption step).
Oral bioavailability is reduced by incomplete absorption and by first-pass hepatic metabolism.
**Plasma protein binding:** only unbound ("free") drug is pharmacologically active and able to cross membranes.
**Lipid solubility:** lipophilic drugs cross membranes more readily and distribute into fatty tissue.
**Tissue perfusion:** highly perfused organs (brain, heart, kidney) receive drug faster than poorly perfused tissue (fat, bone).
Vd is a theoretical volume, not a real anatomic space.
Blood-brain barrier — **Why can some drugs readily enter the CNS while others cannot?** Tight junctions between endothelial cells restrict paracellular movement.
Small, lipophilic, non-ionized drugs cross the BBB more easily than large, polar, or highly protein-bound drugs.
Efflux transporters (like P-glycoprotein) can actively pump some drugs back out of the CNS.
**P-glycoprotein (MDR1)** pumps drugs out of cells in brain, testes, and gut; inhibiting it raises digoxin blood levels.
Ion trapping: weak acids are excreted faster in **alkaline** urine; weak bases faster in **acidic** urine.

children.name: Clinical relevance
facts: Routes that bypass first-pass metabolism: essentially everything except oral — IV, sublingual, inhaled, transdermal, topical, SC, IM.
Sublingual absorption enters systemic venous circulation directly, bypassing the portal vein and the liver's first-pass metabolism; oral dosing passes through the liver first.
Because the liver can inactivate a large fraction of drug first, some drugs are given sublingually or transdermally instead of orally.
A highly polar antibiotic would generally not cross the BBB well — unless the meninges are inflamed, as in meningitis.
Aspirin overdose: sodium bicarbonate alkalinizes blood and urine, reducing aspirin entry into tissues and speeding its renal excretion.

children.name: Drugs named as examples
facts: Large first-pass effect: nitroglycerin, propranolol, morphine — all require higher oral doses (or a non-oral route) to achieve the same systemic exposure as IV.
Very high Vd: digoxin — mostly sequestered in tissue, not floating around in plasma.
Subcutaneous route is common for insulin and heparin.
P-glycoprotein — an efflux transporter at the BBB.

children.name: Exam traps
facts: IV = 100% bioavailable with no absorption phase; oral is less than 100%.
Taking an oral drug with food or on an empty stomach does not bypass first-pass metabolism — sublingual does.
A very high Vd does not mean a big anatomic space — it means the drug is mostly in tissue, not plasma.
Only free (unbound) drug is active and can cross membranes — protein-bound drug cannot.
